## Summary

Adds a new "Host Kernel Tuning" subsection to `docs/configuration/optimization.md` covering two Linux host-level knobs that aren't documented anywhere in the repo today, plus a cross-referencing bullet in `docs/features/kv_offloading_usage.md`'s existing "Tuning Tips" section:

- **CPU frequency governor / C-states / `isolcpus`+`nohz_full`**: the engine-core busy loop and the shared-memory IPC readers between engine core and workers (`vllm/distributed/device_communicators/shm_broadcast.py`'s `SpinCondition`) use a spin-then-block polling strategy. A power-saving governor or deep C-states on the pinned cores (see the existing `--numa-bind`/`--numa-bind-cpus` docs just above this section) undermines that design, adding latency jitter that's easy to misattribute to the GPU or network.
- **`vm.swappiness` / `vm.overcommit_memory`**: hosts using CPU KV offloading (`docs/features/kv_offloading_usage.md`) have the offloaded tier competing with the page cache and other host memory. Default swappiness can swap out offloaded blocks instead of reclaiming page cache first; a permissive overcommit policy combined with a large offload tier can let the OOM killer take a worker process instead of vLLM's own admission control handling it gracefully.

This is docs-only — no code changes, no behavioral changes.

## Why this is not duplicating an existing PR

Ran the duplicate-work checks from `AGENTS.md` before opening this:

```bash
gh pr list --repo vllm-project/vllm --state all --search "cpu governor OR c-state OR cstate"
gh pr list --repo vllm-project/vllm --state all --search "swappiness OR overcommit_memory"
```

Neither search returned anything relevant (results were unrelated CPU-backend feature PRs and one unrelated PR touching a test docstring). Also checked `docs/` directly:

```bash
grep -rn "swappiness\|overcommit_memory\|cpupower\|governor\|c-state\|cstate\|isolcpus\|nohz_full" docs/
```

— zero matches before this change. This is a new section, not a rewrite of existing guidance.

(Separately, while surveying this area I found related NUMA-binding work already in flight — #47336, #51584, #56353 — but none of them touch CPU governor/C-states or memory overcommit/swap, so there's no overlap.)

## Test commands run and results

Docs-only change, so no unit/integration tests apply. What I did verify:

- `git diff` reviewed line-by-line for accuracy against the actual polling implementation in `vllm/distributed/device_communicators/shm_broadcast.py` and the existing `--numa-bind` docs in the same file, so the new section's claims match the real code rather than generic advice.
- All new/changed internal links resolve to real anchors:
  - `../design/arch_overview.md#v1-process-architecture` (already used elsewhere in the same file)
  - `../features/kv_offloading_usage.md#tuning-tips` (confirmed `## Tuning Tips` heading exists)
  - `../configuration/optimization.md#host-kernel-tuning` (the new heading added by this PR)
- Checked the new content against this repo's own `.markdownlint-cli2.yaml` rule overrides (`MD007` 4-space list/admonition indent, `MD013` line-length disabled) by hand, matching the existing `!!! warning`/`!!! important` admonition formatting already used in the same file. Could not run `markdownlint-cli2` itself in my sandbox (Node 18 available, tool requires Node ≥20), so this was a manual check rather than the automated pre-commit hook — flagging this so a reviewer/CI can confirm.
- `grep -n " $"` for trailing whitespace on both changed files: no matches introduced by this change.

detail.title: [Docs] Add host kernel tuning guidance for engine-core polling and KV offload

files.patch:
@@ -467,6 +467,53 @@ CPU underprovisioning particularly impacts:
 
 If you observe that GPU utilization is lower than expected, CPU contention may be the bottleneck. Increasing the number of available CPU cores and even the clock speed can significantly improve end-to-end performance.
 
+### Host Kernel Tuning
+
+Beyond core counts, a few Linux host settings affect the engine core and worker
+processes described above, because vLLM's V1 architecture relies on tight
+polling loops and shared-memory IPC for low latency (see
+[V1 Process Architecture](../design/arch_overview.md#v1-process-architecture)).
+These are host/OS settings, not vLLM flags, so they must be applied outside of
+vLLM itself.
+
+**CPU frequency governor and idle states.** The engine core busy loop and the
+shared-memory IPC readers between engine core and workers use a brief
+spin-then-block polling strategy to avoid wake-up latency on every request. If
+the CPU governor is set to a power-saving policy (for example `powersave`), or
+if deep C-states are enabled on the cores handling these processes, the
+polling loop's effectiveness is undermined: the core either clocks down during
+the spin window or takes longer to wake from a deep idle state, adding latency
+jitter that is easy to misattribute to GPU or network issues. When running a
+latency-sensitive deployment, set the governor to `performance`
+(`cpupower frequency-set -g performance`) and consider limiting deep idle
+states on the cores you pin with `--numa-bind`/`--numa-bind-cpus` (for
+example `cpupower idle-set -D 0`, or the `intel_idle.max_cstate`/
+`processor.max_cstate` kernel boot parameters). `isolcpus` and `nohz_full` can
+further reduce scheduler-tick interference on cores dedicated to the engine
+core or worker processes, at the cost of reduced flexibility for the rest of
+the host workload.
+
+**Memory overcommit and swap for KV offloading.** If you offload KV cache
+blocks to host memory (see
+[KV Offloading Usage Guide](../features/kv_offloading_usage.md)), the
+offloaded tier competes with the page cache and other host memory consumers.
+A default `vm.swappiness` can let the kernel swap out offloaded KV cache pages
+under memory pressure instead of reclaiming page cache first, turning a cache
+miss into a disk-swap stall; setting `vm.swappiness=0` (or a low value) biases
+reclaim away from anonymous/offloaded memory. Conversely, a permissive
+`vm.overcommit_memory` setting combined with a large configured offload tier
+can lead to the OOM killer terminating a worker process under sustained
+pressure rather than vLLM's own admission control rejecting the allocation
+gracefully; size `cpu_bytes_to_use` with real headroom (as already noted under
+[Tuning Tips](../features/kv_offloading_usage.md#tuning-tips)) and verify your
+overcommit policy accounts for it.
+
+!!! note
+    These are general Linux kernel tuning knobs, not vLLM-specific behavior.
+    Validate changes like governor/idle-state settings and `vm.swappiness`
+    against your own workload before applying them broadly, since they affect
+    the whole host, not just vLLM.
+
 ## Attention Backend Selection
 
 vLLM supports multiple attention backends optimized for different hardware and use cases. The backend is automatically selected based on your GPU architecture, model type, and configuration, but you can also manually specify one for optimal performance.

@@ -356,6 +356,7 @@ Implement `SecondaryTierManager` (`vllm/v1/kv_offload/tiering/base.py`) in your
 - `block_size` / `blocks_per_chunk`: larger offloaded chunks reduce per-block bookkeeping overhead but increase the granularity of lookups.
 - FS thread counts: tune `n_read_threads` and `n_write_threads` to the parallelism your storage can sustain. Reads are latency-sensitive on the prefill path, so prefer more read threads when prefill hit rates are high.
 - Sharing `root_dir` across runs: runs with the same model, `block_size`, parallelism layout, and dtype share files under the same `<digest>` subdirectory. Changing any of these produces a new subdirectory; old ones are orphaned but harmless. Delete them to reclaim disk.
+- Host memory pressure: the CPU tier competes with the page cache and other host memory consumers. See [Host Kernel Tuning](../configuration/optimization.md#host-kernel-tuning) for `vm.swappiness`/`vm.overcommit_memory` guidance so the kernel doesn't swap out offloaded blocks or let the OOM killer take a worker process under sustained pressure.
 
 ## Per-Request Selective Offload
